storyboard.claim: Even in our loneliest dark night, other people's voices are still with us.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher stands alone in silhouette while faint grey figures of others hover just behind him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Carries on from the point that existence cannot be untangled from human connection, now into solitude itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: The hovering figures make the ghosts literal — connection persists even when no one is present.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher stands alone with his head lowered as the shapes of other people gather at his back.

storyboard.claim: To find peace, identify which of those ghosts you are arguing with and ask whose judgment it really is.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher turns and points at one grey figure, singling it out from the rest.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the hovering crowd of the last beat into one question you can actually ask.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes identifying the ghost a physical act of isolating a single figure.
storyboard.staging: One finger aimed at one figure: name the voice before you argue with it.

storyboard.claim: The fear of how you will be remembered is out of your control.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man stares at a photograph of himself — the remembrance he cannot direct.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the hardest of the ghosts just raised: your reputation after you are gone.
storyboard.addedInformation: The photograph shows remembrance as something that exists without you, not something you steer.
storyboard.staging: The young man holds a photograph at arm's length and frowns at it: who remembers him is not his to decide.

storyboard.claim: With the groundwork cleared — the past used for present goals, inferiority as a subjective lens — the book's true mechanism is ready.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher closes the book on the old questions and holds it up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Recaps everything settled so far and announces the switch to the book's main tool.
storyboard.addedInformation: Closing the book physically marks the end of the setup before the tool arrives.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher lifts the closed book with both hands: the groundwork is done, the engine comes next.

storyboard.claim: The tool that fixes interpersonal friction is the separation of tasks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A key held up beside the philosopher — the tool that unlocks the whole problem.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the true mechanism the previous beat promised.
storyboard.addedInformation: The key frames the concept as something usable rather than another theory to believe.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher holds a key to the light: this is the tool, not more advice.

storyboard.claim: The hosts stage a scene almost everyone has witnessed: a suffocatingly tense dinner table.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A set dinner table in the kitchen with the philosopher gesturing across it, building the scene.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the named tool to the everyday room where it is needed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the abstraction into a domestic place the viewer recognises on sight.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher indicates the laden table: he is constructing the scene the listeners already know.

storyboard.claim: The teenager slouches, apathetic, refusing homework while picking at a phone.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man slumps at the kitchen table poking a phone while the philosopher glares across at him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Populates the dinner table the previous beat set.
storyboard.addedInformation: The glare and the slump stage both sides of the standoff in a single frame.
storyboard.staging: The young man slouches with the phone, homework untouched: he has simply stopped engaging.

storyboard.claim: The parents' chests tighten with anxiety — they are terrified the child will fail out of school and end up destitute.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher presses a hand to his own chest, face tight with worry, at the same table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the parents' side of the standoff just shown.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the fear a concrete endpoint — school failure and destitution, not a vague mood.
storyboard.staging: Hand pressed to the chest: the parents are terrified of what comes next.

storyboard.claim: The air is resentment, fear and control — a classic power struggle, which the Adlerian approach cuts through with one question.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Both men point at each other across the dinner table: two sides locked in battle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what the dinner-table standoff has actually become.
storyboard.addedInformation: Symmetric pointing turns power struggle into a picture instead of a label.
storyboard.staging: Fingers pointing from both sides of the table: nobody is listening to anybody.

storyboard.claim: Adler's approach cuts the emotional fog with one question: who lives with the consequences?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler raises a single finger and poses the piercing question directly outward.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the piercing question the previous beat promised.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts Adler himself on screen as the source of the test the hosts are using.
storyboard.staging: Adler leans forward, one finger up: who carries the result of this choice?

storyboard.claim: Because the child bears the consequence, studying is the child's task — not the parents'.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher points down the table at the slouching young man: the task sits with the one who lives it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question of the previous beat in three words.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pointing hand assigns ownership visibly — the task physically lands on the child.
storyboard.staging: One firm finger at the teenager: the studying belongs to him.

storyboard.claim: Yelling, threatening, confiscating the phone or bribing all intrude on the child's task — and Adler says every relationship trouble starts from one of two such moves.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The puppeteer icon above a slumping figure: one person pulling the strings of another's work.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the parents' interference for what it is, then generalises it to every relationship.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strings make intrusion read as control rather than care.
storyboard.staging: Adler gestures above the invisible strings: the parents are working a task that is not theirs.

storyboard.claim: All interpersonal troubles come from one of two directions: intruding on other people, or allowing your own tasks to be intruded upon.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two buckets sorting every relationship problem into the two causes Adler names.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sorts the generalisation of the previous beat into its two named causes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the causes as parallel buckets, so the symmetry of the rule reads instantly.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher sorts with two open hands, dropping each complaint into one of two piles.

storyboard.claim: The pushback: the parents are anxious because they love the kid and know better — but Adler says to read that anxiety by its purpose.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man leans in, finger raised, defending the parents' motive at the table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Challenges the rule just sorted: surely a parent's anxiety is care, not intrusion.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the objection into a human defense and sets up the teleological re-reading that follows.
storyboard.staging: The young man presses the point home: of course they are anxious — they love the kid.

storyboard.claim: Read the anxiety teleologically: beneath the love sits the parents' fear of how society and their peers will judge them if the child fails.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher on the street, gesturing at the passers-by who stand in as the judging public.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the love defense by naming the real audience for the parents' anxiety.
storyboard.addedInformation: Moves the judgment out of the family and into the public square where it actually happens.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher indicates the strangers passing behind him: the jury is everybody else.

storyboard.claim: The parents are managing their own task — anxiety and social standing — by forcing the child to complete a different one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher clutches his own chest, then pushes an invisible load across the table at the young man.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the mechanics of the swap the last beat exposed.
storyboard.addedInformation: The physical hand-off makes the boundary violation readable: one person's burden moved onto another.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher gathers something from his own chest and shoves it toward the young man.

storyboard.claim: Forcing someone to change guarantees friction — like sitting in the passenger seat and grabbing the steering wheel from the driver.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An illustration of a car interior: the philosopher leans out of the passenger seat and reaches for the wheel the young man is driving.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the dinner-table violation into the analogy the narration reaches for next.
storyboard.addedInformation: The car makes the consequence of grabbing someone else's task immediate and physical.
storyboard.staging: Passenger and driver fighting over one wheel: control handed to the wrong person.

callout.text: you're going to cause a crash

storyboard.claim: Grab the wheel from the driver and you cause a crash — and the same pattern follows you into the office.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A wrecked car at the roadside, both men shaken and slumped in the dented metal.
storyboard.onScreenText: you're going to cause a crash
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pays off the wheel-grabbing of the last beat, then pivots the argument to the workplace.
storyboard.addedInformation: The wreck shows the guaranteed outcome the narration only states in words.
storyboard.staging: Both men slump in the crashed car: seizing control always ends this way.

storyboard.claim: The unreasonable boss yells, demeans and changes the goalpost constantly, and every commute to work tightens your stomach.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man shrinks at his desk while the philosopher looms over him, shouting and pointing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transfers the car's power struggle into the workplace example the narration introduces.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the daily pattern — one person shouting, one shrinking — instead of describing it.
storyboard.staging: The boss stands over the seated worker, finger jabbing: the same struggle, a new room.

storyboard.claim: The Freudian, etiological reading runs cause to effect: an awful boss is therefore why the work and the career are miserable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step flow drawn across the office: awful boss -> career is miserable.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets out the one-way causality that the next beat will reverse.
storyboard.addedInformation: Draws the chain so the teleological flip has something visible to overturn.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher traces an arrow from a scolding boss to a ruined career.

storyboard.claim: The teleological view reverses the chain: I do not want to face my own failure, so I focus on my awful boss's temper as my excuse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man lifts a mask in front of his face — the temper he hides behind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Flips the chain the previous beat drew: now the boss is the excuse, not the cause.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask shows the excuse is worn on purpose to cover the real motive.
storyboard.staging: The young man holds up a mask and peers around it: the boss's temper is his cover.

storyboard.claim: Apply the separation of tasks and the boss's temper belongs to the boss.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher draws an invisible line in the air and leaves the anger on the far side of it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the excuse of the previous beat with the book's tool.
storyboard.addedInformation: The drawn line makes separation a visible boundary between two people.
storyboard.staging: A flat hand slicing the air: the anger stays where it started.

storyboard.claim: The unreasonable emotions, the yelling and the bad management style are the boss's tasks to deal with, not yours.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher ticks the items off on his fingers and pushes them away from himself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Itemises exactly what the previous beat assigned to the boss.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the boundary into a list the viewer can recognise in their own job.
storyboard.staging: Anger, yelling, bad management — counted off and pushed aside: the boss's problem.

storyboard.claim: Your task is simply to do your work to the best of your ability without lying to yourself — not to manage his mood.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher holds his briefcase squarely in front of him: the work that is actually his.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines your side of the boundary after assigning the boss his.
storyboard.addedInformation: The briefcase draws a hard line around what belongs to you and nothing else.
storyboard.staging: Both hands on the briefcase: do this work and stop managing anybody's feelings.

storyboard.claim: Trying to control his emotions is an intrusion you cannot succeed at; the book says cut the Gordian knot of these tangled relationships.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher makes one chopping motion through the air: stop untangling, cut.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Escalates from boundary to remedy after the do-your-work rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the knot image the next three beats unpack.
storyboard.staging: One clean chop of the hand: some tangles are meant to be severed, not solved.

storyboard.claim: The phrase comes from an ancient legend about Alexander the Great.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher opens his hands in storytelling mode while the young man listens.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pauses the argument to explain the phrase the previous beat dropped in.
storyboard.addedInformation: Flags the phrase as a story, so the next beats read as a parable rather than theory.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher settles into story mode: once, there was a knot nobody could untie.

storyboard.claim: Alexander found an impossibly tangled knot on an ox cart, and an oracle promised rule over all Asia to whoever untied it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man listens with eyebrows lifted as the stakes of the legend land.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the legend the previous beat opened.
storyboard.addedInformation: Carries the oracle's bargain — the prize that made everyone keep trying.
storyboard.staging: The young man's eyebrows rise: untie it and rule Asia.

storyboard.claim: Where others spent days painstakingly untying the ropes, Alexander drew his sword and sliced through it in one swing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher's arm sweeps across in a single hard cut, the sword icon beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the legend's punchline: days of effort replaced by one decisive cut.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sword shows the solution is a cut, not another attempt at untying.
storyboard.staging: One hard swing of the arm: the knot is solved by being severed.

storyboard.claim: Some tangles — an abusive boss, an overbearing parent — are too old and complex to undo slowly with logic or people-pleasing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man sits hunched inside heavy chains: a bond that has been there far too long.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the sword is needed: slow untying cannot work on these.
storyboard.addedInformation: The intact chains say the bind is still on — history, not a puzzle to pick apart.
storyboard.staging: The young man slumps under the chains: some relationships cannot be talked loose.

storyboard.claim: These tangles need a radically new approach — slice through by firmly separating the tasks — before the youth interrupts to challenge it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher holds up a stopping hand as the young man leans in to object.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the knot parable and hands back to the book's tool, then gets cut off.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the break: everything before this was slow untying, everything after is separation.
storyboard.staging: A flat, stopping palm: the old method ends here — and the objection begins.

storyboard.claim: The challenge: if I let my kid fail or stare blankly while my boss screams, isn't that just being a cold, irresponsible, unfeeling jerk?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man leans forward, finger up, firing the objection straight back at the philosopher.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Interrupts the clean solution with its ugliest real-world version.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the fear behind every objection to separation of tasks.
storyboard.staging: The young man jabs the air: isn't that simply walking away in smart language?

storyboard.claim: It does sound like abandonment and selfishness — if you confuse separation with abandonment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A door standing ajar behind the philosopher: the leaving-and-exclusion reading the objection assumes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concedes the force of the objection raised in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door shows what the audience fears separation means: being shut out.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher nods without smiling: yes, from the outside it looks like that.

storyboard.claim: The philosopher is careful: separation of tasks does not mean pushing people away, isolating yourself, or ignoring people when they suffer.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher raises a firm stopping hand as the phrase is struck through on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Rejects the reading the previous beat conceded it resembles.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike shows the phrase is being disqualified, not quoted approvingly.
storyboard.staging: An open palm held up to halt the idea: not that.

storyboard.claim: Intervention is commanding from a position of authority above you — you must study, you need to calm down.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher stands over the seated young man with a commanding hand — authority issued from above.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the first of the two models the whole distinction turns on.
storyboard.addedInformation: The vertical staging makes above you literal instead of metaphorical.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher looms, voice down: do this, now.

storyboard.claim: Assistance is horizontal — standing side by side: I see you are struggling, that is your task, but I am here.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Both men stand shoulder to shoulder facing the same direction, balanced scales beside them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the vertical picture of the previous beat with its horizontal opposite.
storyboard.addedInformation: The level stance and the scales make horizontal visible in a single frame.
storyboard.staging: Level shoulders, equal height: help offered from beside, not from above.

storyboard.claim: Offer resources and support if asked — you lead the horse to water, but you do not force it to drink.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher holds out a wrapped gift: help available, never pushed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Spells out what side-by-side assistance actually looks like in practice.
storyboard.addedInformation: The gift frames support as something handed over rather than imposed.
storyboard.staging: An open-handed offer: take it if you want it.

storyboard.claim: You only have the power to control your side of the ledger — offer support, never carry their burden for them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher draws a vertical line down the middle of the frame and keeps one hand planted on his own half.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Redraws the same boundary as an accounting line right after the gift of support.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ledger split makes your side a place the viewer can point to.
storyboard.staging: One hand on his own half: the rest stays with them.

storyboard.claim: Adult stress is almost always a massive teetering stack of other people's tasks that you voluntarily picked up.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man struggles to balance a wobbling pile of papers that reaches past his chin.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the ledger line keeps getting crossed: we collect what is not ours.
storyboard.addedInformation: The teetering pile shows the stress as borrowed material rather than your own work.
storyboard.staging: Arms full, papers tilting: every sheet belongs to somebody else.

storyboard.claim: That teetering stack leads straight back to the show's recurring phrase.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher sets the pile down and turns toward the camera: here comes the line again.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from the image of borrowed stress back to the method itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Signals a return, so the next beat reads as the payoff rather than a new idea.
storyboard.staging: The papers hit the table and the philosopher looks up: back to the question.

storyboard.claim: When the crushing weight lands in your chest, stop and ask whose task it is — keep what is yours and hand the rest back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A boulder sits on the philosopher's chest; he points outward, splitting the weight between people.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the refrain the previous beat announced, as the move to make the next time the weight arrives.
storyboard.addedInformation: The boulder gives the chest weight a shape and the pointing shows the response.
storyboard.staging: Hand on chest under the rock, the other hand sending it away: mine stays, the rest goes.
